chunks.document_content: However, recent studies have also suggested that intensive therapies that result in rapid reductions in Hemoglobin A1C (HbA1C), such as with glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, can be associated with initial worsening of DR at least in the early stages but may ultimately be protective in late or advanced stages [9-12]. Of note, GLP-1 agonist use has been asso­ ciated with a 2-fold increase in incidence of neovascular age-related macular degeneration among patients with diabetes [13]. Despite their widespread use in clinical practice, anti-VEGF therapies are limited by several key challenges. One major drawback is their relatively short intraocu­ lar half-life, which often necessitates frequent intravit­ real injections to sustain therapeutic efficacy [21]. This repeated administration contributes to the high overall cost of treatment and poses significant accessibility bar­ riers for some patient populations [24]. Additionally, the need for repeated injections increases the risk of injec­ tion-related complications, such as endophthalmitis, a rare but potentially vision-threatening infection [25]. Furthermore, anti-VEGF therapy does not elicit a uni­ form response across all patient populations [26]. The proportion of non-responders after three injections has been demonstrated to be as high as 65% [26]. These non-responders only had a 3.2-letter gain in best visual acuity at 12 months following anti-VEGF treatment compared to 12.8-letter gain in responders [26]. Consequently, pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP), a form of laser therapy, can be used as an alternative or in combination with anti-VEGF agents, depending on patient preference and DME status [27]. However, even with this approximately 32-39% of PDR patients develop vitreous hemorrhage In DR visual symptoms progress from normal vision to blurred or distorted vison and impaired color perception, ultimately culminating in complete blindness in severe stages of DR [8, 14]. The early stage is referred to as non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) which includes several structural anatomic retinal alterations, such as the loss of retinal pericytes, thickening of capillary basement membrane, and microaneurysm formation [15]. Pericytes are mural cells embedded in the basement membrane of small blood vessels, where they play a crucial role in vas­ cular stability and blood flow regulation; their degenera­ tion weakens the vessel walls and disrupts microvascular integrity [16]. These changes occur alongside neuronal dysfunction and impaired retinal blood flow, even before clinical signs appear [17]. NPDR is often asymptomatic or accompanied by minor visual changes, however pro­ gressive pericyte loss and microvascular occlusion lead after PRP and may require vitrectomy as an additional surgical intervention [28]. Given the limited durability, high cost, procedural risks, and suboptimal efficacy of current anti-VEGF therapies there is an urgent and com­ pelling need to explore alternative therapeutic strategies for DR. Recently, Lamivudine, an inflammasome inhibi­ tor traditionally used to treat human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), has demonstrated efficacy comparable to -or potentially exceeding- that of VEGF inhibitors in improv­ ing visual acuity [29]. However, this therapeutic appli­ cation has not yet received FDA approval and requires further validation.

chunks.document_content: The role of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR/ErbB1) in diabetic retinopathy and its therapeutic implications Marwan Malluhi1†, Dina Tluli1† and Saghir Akhtar1* Abstract Background Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a major cause of preventable vision loss worldwide and arises from the convergence of chronic inflammation, oxidative injury, and metabolic dysregulation that ultimately compromises vascular and neuronal integrity of the retina. Although intravitreal anti-VEGF agents have improved the management of DR, significant limitations such as incomplete therapeutic response, repeated administration and high cost underscore the need for alternative or adjunctive strategies. Main body Emerging preclinical evidence suggests that dysregulated signaling via the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) plays a critical role in DR pathogenesis. EGFR and some of its ligands are expressed across multiple retinal cell types and play important roles in normal development and in regulating homeostasis in adult retinas. However, in hyperglycemia/diabetes enhanced EGFR signaling promotes vascular hyperpermeability, pericyte loss, glial reactivity, inflammatory amplification, and pro-fibrotic remodeling that contributes to both early microvascular dysfunction and later proliferative changes in experimental models. Several preclinical studies indicate that pharmacologic blockade of EGFR or downstream signaling pathways attenuates angiogenesis, inflammation, and gliosis in models of DR. Conclusions These emerging preclinical findings implicate EGFR as a promising therapeutic target to complement or extend beyond VEGF-centered approaches. Further validation of the role of EGFR and its ligands in mediating retinal pathology in clinically relevant models will be essential for advancing EGFR-targeted interventions toward clinical translation. chunks.document_content: 4.4 Empathy Readability remained a shared limitation across models. Gemini generated comparatively more readable responses, whereas Doubao showed greater reading difficulty; however, all models produced text above recommended patient-reading levels. This indicates that read­ ability is not only a model-specific weakness but a broader limitation of LLM-generated medical education. This finding is consistent with prior work showing that freely available online DR information is often difficult to read and may exceed recommended reading levels (51). Similar concerns have also been reported in broader audits of medical chatbot responses (50). Empathy showed clearer variation than factual accuracy, suggest­ ing that patient-centered communication is a distinct dimension of LLM performance. Copilot performed relatively well in empathy, whereas Doubao and Perplexity scored lower. This difference may reflect variation in default tone, response length, emotional acknowl­ edgement, and whether the model explicitly recognizes patient con­ cerns before providing factual information. In DR, empathy is clinically relevant because patients may fear blindness, injections, laser treatment, surgery, pregnancy-related worsening, or loss of independence. This issue has direct implications for health equity. Patients with DR need to understand asymptomatic disease progression, screening intervals, systemic risk-factor control, warning symptoms, anti-VEGF injections, laser treatment, pregnancy-related risk, and long-term follow-up. If responses require advanced reading ability, they may fail to support patients with limited health literacy. Future patient-facing LLM systems should use shorter sentences, plain-language explana­ tions, clear action-oriented advice, and simple definitions of unavoid­ able medical terms such as diabetic macular edema, proliferative diabetic retinopathy, anti-VEGF therapy, and panretinal photocoagu­ lation. Readability improvement should not come at the cost of clinical accuracy or safety escalation. Previous studies have reported that AI-generated responses can sometimes be perceived as empathetic in written medical question-answer settings (7, 9). Nevertheless, empathy in medical AI should not be reduced to warmth or reassurance. Over-reassurance may become unsafe if it minimizes sudden symptoms, delays referral, or overstates the reversibility of advanced disease. For DR patient education, the ideal response should acknowledge anxiety, explain the issue clearly, and provide appropriate next steps. Future evaluations should there­ fore assess "safe empathy," meaning communication that is supportive and patient-centered while still maintaining clinical caution. 4.5 Information quality, reliability, and transparency 4.7 Clinical and public health implications The results for DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA benchmark criteria, and GQS show that information quality cannot be fully captured by global impression alone. Perplexity performed relatively well on DISCERN and JAMA, while Copilot, Gemini, and Perplexity performed well on EQIP. In contrast, GQS differences were smaller and did not fully align with structured reliability or transparency metrics. A response may therefore appear fluent, organized, and useful while still lacking ade­ quate source attribution, balanced treatment information, disclosure, currency, or explanation of uncertainty. The findings have practical implications for how LLMs may be incorporated into DR education. They do not support selecting a single consumer chatbot as an autonomous educator on the basis of an overall score or model ranking. A safer implementation model would use LLM-generated text as a draft, navigation aid, or supple­ mentary explanation within clinician- or educator-supervised work­ flows.

chunks.document_content: Eyes that had previously received anti-VEGF therapy, intravitreal corticosteroid treatment, or focal/grid laser photocoagulation for DME were excluded. The diagno­ sis of DME was based on clinical examination and opti­ cal coherence tomography (OCT) findings. Eyes were excluded if baseline best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) data were unavailable or if significant ocular comorbidi­ ties that could affect visual acuity were present, including advanced glaucoma, dense cataract, or corneal opacity. Both eyes from the same patient were included if they met the eligibility criteria, reflecting routine clinical practice. Treatment switching represents another important aspect of DME management in real-world settings. A considerable proportion of patients exhibit subopti­ mal anatomical or functional response to initial anti-VEGF therapy, necessitating a switch to alternative agents. Although previous studies suggest that switch­ ing may provide additional benefit in selected cases, evi­ dence regarding optimal timing, patient selection, and Treatment protocol All eyes initially received three consecutive monthly intravitreal injections of bevacizumab as a loading phase, in accordance with institutional treatment protocols and reimbursement policies. Following the loading phase, patients were managed using a pro re nata (PRN) regi­ men. Retreatment decisions were based on OCT find­ ings and functional assessment. Criteria for retreatment included the presence of persistent or recurrent intra­ retinal or subretinal fluid, increased central macular thickness, or deterioration in BCVA compared with the previous visit. Patients were followed at monthly inter­ vals, during which OCT imaging was performed to guide retreatment decisions. and timing; and the association between injection num­ ber and visual acuity change.

chunks.document_content: The fact that NRG was detected in both the vitreous and fibrovas­ cular membranes suggests a potential role in neuroglial remodeling [146]. Since in cell culture models, NRG1-ErbB signaling promotes neurite outgrowth and neuro­ nal survival in dorsal root ganglia and motoneurons [155, EGFR and other ErbB receptors are expressed across multiple cell types in the healthy retina (Fig. 2) and serve essential physiological roles in regulating prolif­ eration, differentiation, migration, and survival. While EGFR signaling is required for normal retinal develop­ ment, function, and repair [159], its chronic overactiva­ tion is directly associated with the development of DR in preclinical models. Although longitudinal studies mapping EGFR expression across distinct stages of dis­ ease progression are lacking, available evidence suggests that overactivation occurs early in the disease course, as EGFR inhibition appears to be most efficacious at this stage [49]. Early pharmacological targeting may therefore warrant investigation during the initial non-proliferative stages, where EGFR inhibition could reduce pro-inflam­ matory cytokine release, limit pericyte loss, and attenuate BRB disruption before irreversible neovascularization, neurodegeneration, and fibrosis are established. In this context, EGFR-targeted therapy could represent a pre­ ventative or disease-modifying approach, complement­ ing existing anti-VEGF and anti-inflammatory strategies, though robust preclinical and clinical validation is an essential prerequisite.

chunks.document_content: Introduction new therapeutic targets and developing more effica­ cious treatment strategies have become particularly urgent. Diabetic Retinopathy (DR), as one of the most com­ mon microvascular complications of diabetes, affects approximately 34.6% of individuals living with dia­ betes, with 30% progressing to varying degrees of vis­ ual impairment (Wang et al., 2024). The pathological characteristics primarily include capillary degener­ ation, loss of pericytes, and vessel leakage (Liu et al., 2023). At present, the therapeutic strategies for DR mainly focus on systemic treatment, vitrectomy, ret­ inal photocoagulation, and intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF inhibitors (Yamato et al., 2024). While these treatments primarily address advanced DR, their efficacy is limited for early-stage disease. They can also result in many adverse reactions, including pos­ sible permanent loss of peripheral vision and worsen­ ing macular edema (Hu et al., 2024). Thus, exploring As intrinsic resident immune cells of the retina, microglia maintain homeostatic distribution under physiological conditions and participate in the dynamic equilibrium of the retinal microenvironment by constantly surveilling the local microenvironment, clearing metabolic waste, and stabilizing synaptic structures (Guo et al., 2022). Exposure to high glucose and oxidative stress triggers reactive activation of ret­ inal microglia, accompanied by enhanced secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1b, IL-6, and TNF-a.
